name: Medellín
note: City of Eternal Spring 22°C. Laureles > El Poblado for longer stays.
description: Medellín, capital of Antioquia and Colombia's second city, fills the Aburrá Valley in the Andes at about 1,495 m. It has the country's only metro, and homicides have fallen about 95% since the cartel years of the 1980s and early 1990s. A month here is affordable: Numbeo puts a cappuccino near COP 9,760, a cheap restaurant meal at COP 26,000 and a monthly transit pass at COP 248,000. Metro lines A and B, the Metrocable gondolas, the Ayacucho tram and Metroplús buses share one network. Coworkings include Tinkko and Selina in El Poblado (roughly $120–220 a month) and Epicentro in Laureles ($100–150). Ookla measured Medellín's median fixed broadband at 66.5 Mbps in April 2025. Clocks follow Colombia Time (UTC−5), and Colombia offers a digital nomad visa. It is called the city of eternal spring: highs stay near 28°C and lows near 18°C all year. Rain peaks in April and in October–November; June to August is the drier stretch. Trade-offs: safety varies sharply by area, with poorer hillside districts and much of the centre best avoided at night, and a central one-bedroom runs about COP 3.33 million (about $1,040) a month.

neighbourhoods.name: El Poblado (Provenza & Parque Lleras)
neighbourhoods.about: Hillside commune of towers, restaurants and the Parque Lleras bar zone
neighbourhoods.description: El Poblado, Comuna 14, climbs the south-east slope of the valley from the Medellín River. It takes its name from the first Spanish settlement of 1616 and is now the city's main business and wealthy residential district, with about 129,000 residents across 24 barrios. Most visitors stay in the streets around Parque Lleras, the Zona Rosa between Parque El Poblado and Parque Lleras, and neighbouring Provenza, where Carrera 35 is lined with restaurants, cafés and bars. Coworkings such as Tinkko and Selina are here. Wikipedia notes almost no homicides in El Poblado, and Wikivoyage treats it as the one area safe to walk at night. It is also the priciest part of the city, and Parque Lleras is busy and loud most nights.
watch_out: Parque Lleras is loud on weekend nights
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Poblado and Aguacatala stations on Metro Line A sit at the foot of the slope; most hillside streets need a taxi or a steep walk.

neighbourhoods.name: Laureles–Estadio
neighbourhoods.about: Planned, flat residential district west of the river near the stadium
neighbourhoods.description: Laureles–Estadio, Comuna 11, lies west of the Medellín River between Robledo to the north and Belén to the south. It was laid out as a planned district from the 1930s onward and is mostly home to better-off households. Its streets are flatter and calmer than El Poblado's. The Estadio area holds the city's main stadiums and sports grounds, Carrera 70 has many of the city's salsa clubs, and Avenida 33 is another bar strip. Atom House, Epicentro and Casa Redonda are coworkings here. Rents run well below El Poblado, which has made it a common choice for longer stays. Nightlife is more local and spread out, and there are fewer English-speaking services than across the river.
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Metro Line B runs along the district with Suramericana, Estadio and Floresta stations, linking to Line A at San Antonio.

neighbourhoods.name: Envigado
neighbourhoods.about: Separate town just south of El Poblado with a traditional main square
neighbourhoods.description: Envigado is its own municipality, bordering El Poblado to the north and Sabaneta to the south, with about 200,000 people. It is known for keeping Paisa traditions and for one of the highest standards of living in Colombia. Life centres on the Parque Principal Marceliano Vélez and the streets around it. Otraparte, the house of the writer Fernando González, is now a museum and cultural centre with gardens. It is quieter and cheaper than El Poblado while staying close to it. The town's past is tied to Pablo Escobar, but the Aburrá Valley now has one of Colombia's lowest homicide rates. Evenings are calmer, with fewer late-night bars.
watch_out: Metro station is about 2 km from Otraparte and the hillside
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Envigado station on Metro Line A serves the town, a few stops south of Poblado; buses and taxis cover the hillside.

neighbourhoods.name: Belén
neighbourhoods.about: Large south-western commune around Cerro Nutibara and Pueblito Paisa
neighbourhoods.description: Belén, Comuna 16, is one of Medellín's largest and most populous communes, with about 217,500 residents in 2024. It lies south of Laureles–Estadio and west of the river, mixing older residential streets with modern shopping centres. Its main landmark is Cerro Nutibara, the hill topped by Pueblito Paisa, a small replica of an Antioquian village with city views, and the Carlos Vieco open-air theatre that hosts the International Poetry Festival. Belén is a local, working-to-middle-class area with few tourists and rents below Laureles. The southern edge borders the airport side of the city, where Wikipedia reports higher crime rates.
watch_out: Crime is higher towards the south-west and the airport
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Metroplús Line 1 runs through Belén from its University of Medellín terminus; Industriales station on Line A is the closest for Nutibara.

neighbourhoods.name: La Candelaria (Centro)
neighbourhoods.about: Historic downtown of Botero sculptures, churches and Junín street
neighbourhoods.description: La Candelaria, Comuna 10, is Medellín's founding and historic centre, where the town of Our Lady of Candelaria was laid out in 1675 around today's Parque Berrío. It is the city's commercial core and its busiest metro interchange. Plaza Botero has large Fernando Botero sculptures in front of the Museo de Antioquia, which holds many of his paintings. Nearby are the Basílica de la Candelaria from 1767, the brick Metropolitan Cathedral on Parque Bolívar and the pedestrian Junín street. It is best seen by day. Wikivoyage advises avoiding most of the inner city at night, and the Spanish Wikipedia notes heavy traffic pollution in the centre. Few visitors choose to sleep here.
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Parque Berrío and San Antonio stations on Metro Line A serve the centre; San Antonio also connects to Line B and the Ayacucho tram.

neighbourhoods.name: Sabaneta
neighbourhoods.about: Colombia's smallest municipality, at the valley's southern end
neighbourhoods.description: Sabaneta is a separate municipality at the south end of the Aburrá Valley, bordered by Envigado, Itagüí, La Estrella and Caldas. At 15 km², it is the smallest municipality in Colombia. It draws visitors from across the metro area at weekends for its restaurants and nightlife, and Wikivoyage notes it has not caught on with foreigners, so it suits people who want a local scene. La Romera ecological park lies in its hills. Rents are among the lowest of the areas here, and the metro reaches it. The trade-off is distance: El Poblado and the centre are a long ride north, and there are few services aimed at foreigners.
watch_out: Long ride to the centre and El Poblado
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Sabaneta station on Metro Line A, opened in 2012 near Calle 67 Sur, links the town to Envigado, Poblado and the centre.

neighbourhoods.name: Comuna 13 (San Javier)
neighbourhoods.about: Hillside commune known for graffiti tours and outdoor escalators
neighbourhoods.description: Comuna 13, also called San Javier, is a commune of about 160,000 people on the western hills, made of brick houses stacked up steep slopes. It suffered heavily from violence linked to drug trafficking, paramilitaries and military operations. It is now one of the city's main attractions. The tourist area is in Barrio Independencias along Carrera 109, about 1.3 km from San Javier metro station, where outdoor escalators climb past murals, bars, food stalls and souvenir kiosks. Wikivoyage describes it as fairly peaceful as of 2025, and most people visit on a guided or self-guided walk by day. It is a place to visit rather than to stay.
watch_out: Visit by day and stay on the main tourist route
neighbourhoods.getting_around: San Javier station at the end of Metro Line B is the gateway; Metrocable Line J climbs from it to La Aurora.

neighbourhoods.name: Laureles
neighbourhoods.about: Local vibe, cheaper, preferred by long-stayers

best_season: Dec–Feb and Jul–Aug (the drier windows). Rains peak Apr–May and Oct–Nov, usually as afternoon storms.
time_zone: UTC−5 year-round — matches US Eastern in winter, 1h behind in US summer.
sim_cost: Claro or Tigo ≈ $8–12/mo (COP ~40–60k) with 20–40 GB. Coverage strong.
english_level: Limited outside El Poblado; Laureles runs on Spanish.
getting_around: Excellent metro and Metrocable; Uber and DiDi are cheap. Scooters less common for visitors.
scene: Very large — a top-3 Latin America nomad hub, dense in El Poblado and Laureles.

name: Bogotá
note: Altitude 2,640m. Gold Museum is world-class. Best to acclimatize first.
best_season: Dec–Mar (the drier season). At 2,600 m it is cool year-round — pack for 10–19°C any month.
flight_from_miami: ≈3h45 direct to BOG, several flights a day.
time_zone: UTC−5 year-round — matches US Eastern in winter, 1h behind in US summer.
english_level: Limited to moderate — better in the north (Chicó, Chapinero).
getting_around: TransMilenio buses plus Uber/DiDi; traffic is heavy and the city is sprawling.
scene: Medium — more business travellers and students than lifestyle nomads.

name: Cartagena
note: Very hot 30°C+. Best Oct–Apr. Expensive by Colombian standards.
best_season: Dec–Apr (dry trade-wind season). May–Nov is hotter, humid, with downpours.
time_zone: UTC−5 year-round — matches US Eastern in winter, 1h behind in US summer.
sim_cost: Claro ≈ $8–12/mo. Coverage strong in the city.
english_level: Moderate in the Old Town and Bocagrande; Spanish elsewhere.
getting_around: The Old Town is fully walkable; taxis and Uber cover the rest.
scene: Small to medium — more holidaymakers and remote workers passing through than long-stay nomads.
